title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.
target_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
contributions: A graph-based section scheduler that organizes document generation around a document graph to improve coherence.
An evidence-injection protocol and evidence-aware prompts that attach and verify citations per section.
An audit-friendly, strict JSON output schema and a LaTeX assembly workflow (refs.bib) for traceability and post-hoc review.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Motivate the challenge of reliable long-form scientific writing with large language models, state the research question—how does graph-guided sectioning affect coherence and citation quality?—and give a high-level overview of the graph-guided prompting workflow and conservative claim policy (always cite sources).

sections.title: Related Work
sections.summary: Review prior approaches to long-form generation, structured prompting, citation-aware generation, and document planning. Contrast linear prompting baselines and citation verification techniques, emphasizing gaps addressed by a graph-aware approach.

sections.title: Methods
sections.summary: Detail the graph construction (section graph and dependencies), the JSON schema for section outputs, evidence retrieval and ranking, evidence-aware prompt templates, leaf-first generation and assembly rules, and the LaTeX + refs.bib assembly process. Include conservative validation checks and failure modes.

sections.title: Experiments
sections.summary: Describe experimental setup: two topical domains, baseline linear prompting comparator, datasets (internal notes and a small curated PDF set if available), and evaluation protocol. Specify metrics: citation coverage, hallucination rate (unsupported assertions), and reviewer score.

sections.title: Results
sections.summary: Report quantitative outcomes on citation coverage, hallucination rates, and reviewer scores, with qualitative examples illustrating error modes and successful evidence integration. Emphasize conservative interpretation of improvements and per-topic variability.

sections.title: Discussion
sections.summary: Analyze why graph-guided scheduling affects coherence and citation placement, limitations (dataset scale, domain transfer, reliance on retrieval quality), and implications for auditability and reproducibility. Propose mitigations and future extensions.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Summarize contributions and findings, restate emphasis on conservative claims and mandatory citations, and outline next steps for larger-scale evaluation and community-shared datasets and tools.
